label: Well-Connected Graduate Male
summary: This profile represents men with graduate-level education who report notably low levels of loneliness, depressive symptoms, and anxiety, alongside relatively light daily social-media use averaging around 2.8 hours. With a UCLA-8 loneliness score near 0.89, a PHQ-9 depression score of approximately 0.32, and a GAD-7 anxiety score of 0.0, these respondents exhibit strong psychological well-being. Their moderate social-media engagement (1–3 hours daily) suggests balanced digital habits that do not encroach on mental health.

behavior_markers: Low loneliness scores indicating strong social connectedness
Minimal depressive symptomatology (PHQ-9 near zero)
Absence of anxiety symptoms (GAD-7 score of 0.0)
Light and controlled social-media usage averaging approximately 2.8 hours per day
Balanced digital engagement without signs of excessive screen time

label: Lonely & Distressed Light User
summary: This profile captures highly educated women who report elevated loneliness, depressive symptoms, and anxiety symptoms despite relatively light daily social-media use (approximately 1–3 hours). Their mental health burden is notably high across all three measured dimensions—loneliness (UCLA-8 mean ≈ 1.55), depression (PHQ-9 mean ≈ 1.60), and anxiety (GAD-7 mean ≈ 1.88)—suggesting that psychological distress in this group is not driven by heavy social-media engagement. The profile comprises 66 respondents from the training split.

label: Digitally Immersed & Emotionally Strained
summary: This profile represents highly educated women who spend more than 5 hours daily on social media and report elevated levels of loneliness, depressive symptoms, and anxiety. Their heavy social-media engagement co-occurs with above-average scores on loneliness (UCLA-8 mean ≈ 1.88), depression (PHQ-9 mean ≈ 2.05), and notably high anxiety (GAD-7 mean = 3.0), suggesting a pattern of psychological distress alongside intensive digital social activity.

tone: Concerned and empirically grounded; highlights the convergence of heavy social-media use with elevated emotional vulnerability in a highly educated female subgroup

label: Socially Connected Heavy Scroller
summary: This profile represents respondents who report low loneliness, low depressive symptoms, and low anxiety despite spending nearly five hours per day on social media. Their psychological well-being scores are consistently below scale midpoints (UCLA-8 loneliness mean ≈ 1.20, PHQ-9 depression mean ≈ 0.81, GAD-7 anxiety mean ≈ 0.74), suggesting that their heavy social-media engagement coexists with—or may even support—positive mental health outcomes. The profile is the largest training-split cluster (n = 152), indicating this pattern is relatively common in the sample.
demographic_anchor: Female, graduate-level education or above, reporting 3–5 hours of daily social-media use (midpoint ≈ 4.8 hours)
behavior_markers: Heavy daily social-media use averaging approximately 4.8 hours

tone: Balanced and empirically cautious; highlights the coexistence of high social-media engagement with low psychological distress without implying causation

label: Well-Adjusted Graduate Male with Light Social-Media Use
summary: This profile represents a group of 186 respondents characterized by notably low levels of loneliness, depressive symptoms, and anxiety symptoms, combined with relatively light daily social-media use. Their mean loneliness score (UCLA-8 ≈ 1.18), depression score (PHQ-9 ≈ 0.69), and anxiety score (GAD-7 ≈ 0.75) all fall well below clinical thresholds, suggesting generally positive psychological well-being. Their average daily social-media consumption centers around 1.5 hours (1–3 hours range), indicating moderate and controlled engagement with digital platforms.
